source.citation: Helsel, D.R. and Hirsch, R.M. (2002). Statistical Methods in Water Resources. Techniques of Water-Resources Investigations of the U.S. Geological Survey, book 4, chapter A3 (superseded by Techniques and Methods 4-A3, 2020)
source.locator: sect. 3.3.1, example 2, pp. 71-72: the 25 arsenic concentrations [ppb] of groundwaters of southeastern New Hampshire (Boudette and others, 1985), median 19, the 13th; x' = 7 from table B5 (0.022, nearest alpha/2 = 0.025), R_l = 8 and R_u = 25 - 7 = 18 (eqs. 3.2-3.3): 4.8 <= C_0.5 <= 110 at alpha = 0.044

conventions: the 25 concentrations as the annual values of one percentage in 25 years: the formula is the interval of the median of any independent sample, and the bounds and the median are values of the sample, printed as given

the tail of x' = 7, P(B <= 7) = 0.0216 for B ~ Bin(25, 1/2), is the one nearest alpha/2 = 0.025 and also below it, so the source's rule and the spec's (each tail at most (1 - c) / 2) give the same pair, k = 8 and N + 1 - k = 18, of coverage 0.9567
the large-sample ranks of eqs. 3.4-3.5 on p. 73, 7.6 and 18.4 rounded, give the same pair

the 2020 edition (Helsel, Hirsch, Ryberg, Archfield and Gilroy, Techniques and Methods 4-A3, example 3.1, p. 63) prints [4.8, 100] from qbinom's ranks 8 and 17 while stating the coverage sum(dbinom(8:17, 25, 0.5)) = 0.9567, which is that of the 8th to the 18th value: its upper rank is one too low, so it is no second source of this case
